docker.title: Docker labels
docker.intro: PROXY64 reads the containers on this Docker host through the Docker API and creates proxy hosts from their labels – no form needed. Names, scheme and target come from the labels; everything else (CDN64 online, access list, protection, certificate …) is set on the host and kept when the container is restarted or updated.
docker.on_hint: Containers with node64.proxy.host become proxy hosts. When a container (or the label) is removed, PROXY64 deletes the host after 2 minutes, including its CDN64 online registration.
docker.traefik_hint: For switchers: Host(…) rules of Traefik routers, port and scheme of the service and traefik.docker.network. Middlewares, path rules and tls.certresolver are not used. If a container has its own labels, only those apply.
docker.host_hint: Empty = default (like Docker monitoring). Allowed: unix:///path, tcp://host:port or http(s)://host:port, e.g. a docker-socket-proxy. Only the Docker host Node64 runs on.
docker.cert_none: Don't request one (matching existing certificate, otherwise HTTP only)
docker.cert_hint: For newly created Docker hosts PROXY64 requests a certificate this way. Without a choice the host uses a matching existing certificate (e.g. wildcard), otherwise it stays on HTTP.
docker.tos_hint: Once here instead of per container; applies to all Let's Encrypt certificates.
docker.error_hint: Is the socket mounted and may Node64 read it (group_add with the socket's group)? With a docker-socket-proxy set CONTAINERS=1 and EVENTS=1. Until the list can be read again, PROXY64 deletes no hosts.
docker.off_hint: Switched off. Switch on so PROXY64 reads the containers.
docker.empty: No container with node64.proxy.* or Traefik labels found.
docker.form_hint: Comes from the Docker labels of container {name}.
docker.form_access: Comes from the Docker label (access list "{name}").
docker.form_locked: Names, scheme and target are therefore locked; everything else can be set here and is kept.
docker.help_labels: Put labels on the container, PROXY64 creates the host by itself:
docker.help_network: Network: PROXY64 connects to the container directly. Easiest is a shared Docker network for Node64 and the container (or Node64 with network_mode: host); with several networks set node64.proxy.network.
docker.help_socket: Socket: mount /var/run/docker.sock read-only (with group_add of the socket's group) or, safer, put a docker-socket-proxy with CONTAINERS=1 and EVENTS=1 in front. PROXY64 only sends GET requests.

The lists are refreshed every 30 minutes and cached locally; private networks are never listed.

hp.title: Honeypot64
hp.hint: PROXY64 can work together with the Honeypot64 module of this node. Each point can be switched on separately and is off by default.
hp.decoy_hint: Requests without a matching host (IP only, foreign domain, unknown name) go to the web decoy of Honeypot64 instead of the default page. Unknown names get the fallback certificate.
hp.decoy_missing: Honeypot64 does not offer a web decoy right now – until then the default page applies.
hp.decoy_visible: The node then answers unknown requests visibly (login page, fallback certificate) – even if the default page is set to “close connection”.
hp.access_hint: For each request only metadata goes to Honeypot64 (IP, host, method, path without query, status, failed login) – never content. The honeypot evaluates it with its own rules.
hp.access_missing: Honeypot64 does not evaluate accesses right now.
hp.block: Block attackers from the honeypot immediately
hp.block_hint: IPs that stand out in the honeypot are blocked by PROXY64 for all hosts and streams – without waiting for the v64 blocklist. Private addresses, blocklist exceptions and trusted proxies of the hosts are never blocked. The list is kept in memory (at most 50,000 entries).
hp.block_wanted: Switched on by Honeypot64 ("Block detected attackers in PROXY64").
hp.needs: Needs the Honeypot64 module (switched on under Settings → Modules).
hp.err_hours: The duration must be between 1 and 720 hours.
hp.wanted: Honeypot64 runs with the “Only via PROXY64” preset: it opens no ports of its own, the decoy is on and gets the requests below.
hp.route: Also send requests recognised as malicious to the decoy
hp.route_hint: Instead of 403 the honeypot decoy answers these requests – attackers notice nothing, the honeypot collects more. Only while the decoy is active and only for HTTP(S); TCP/UDP streams and TLS passthrough still reject.
hp.route_honeypot: attackers reported by the honeypot (instant block)
hp.route_exploit: exploit patterns (“Block Common Exploits” on the host)
hp.route_ai_bot: AI bots and scanners (blocked on the host)
hp.route_never: Overload (too many requests or connections) never goes to the decoy – that is protection, not an attack.

lim.title: DoS protection (denial of service) – overload protection
lim.hint: Limits connections and requests per IP address (IPv6 per /64), like HAProxy. Protects the node and every service behind the proxy against request flooding and many connections from one address. Addresses that hit the limits too often are rejected for a few minutes right when they connect. Exempt are the home network (if enabled), the trusted proxies of the hosts (e.g. Cloudflare; the real client IP counts there) and the blocklist exceptions. The defaults are fine for browsers, apps and sync clients.
lim.exempt_lan: Never limit the home network (private addresses)
lim.conn_rate_hint: ten times as many for a short while, checked before TLS.
lim.req_rate_hint: sustained; above that the answer is 429.
lim.req_burst_hint: allowed for a short while, e.g. when loading many images.
lim.target_conns_hint: requests to the service behind a proxy host; more wait up to 10 s, then 503. WebSockets do not count.
lim.max_conns_hint: protects the node itself. Small devices such as a Raspberry Pi rather 2000–3000, a NAS or PC up to 10000.
lim.zero_hint: 0 = this limit off. Single hosts can be exempted under Advanced (e.g. an API used by many devices behind one address).
lim.rejected_hint: Connections and requests since PROXY64 started that hit limits or bans
lim.reset_confirm: Set all limits to their defaults?
lim.err_range: Check the values: whole numbers from 0 only (ban at most 7 days).

online.ex1_text: The servers are just postmen: they read the name and pass the encrypted connection through the tunnel. Decryption happens only in your node; certificate and key stay here. The right choice for almost everything.
online.ex1_art:
Visitor ══HTTPS══► srv07 / srv08 ══tunnel══► Node64 ──► service
                   reads the name only,      TLS ends here,
                   does not decrypt          your certificate
online.ex2_text: The servers open the connection (their own Let's Encrypt certificate), check it and filter right there: blocklists, limits per IP, HTTP/3. Good for a small upload or lots of unwanted traffic. Not for hosts with "TLS pass-through".
online.ex2_art:
Visitor ══HTTPS══► srv07 / srv08 ══tunnel══► Node64 ──► service
                   TLS ends here,            request with real
                   blocklists, IP limits     visitor IP
online.ex3_text: The servers go straight to your target without a tunnel – the target must be reachable from the internet. With caching on the servers and a port mapper. Does not run through the container and is set up on the website:
online.ex3_art:
Visitor ══HTTPS══► srv07 / srv08 ══internet══► your target
                   cache, port mapper          publicly reachable,
                                               no Node64, no tunnel

dnscheck.link: DNS-01 check: test paths, own resolvers
dnscheck.title: DNS-01 check
dnscheck.intro: Before Let's Encrypt validates, the node checks that the TXT record is visible in DNS: first directly at the nameservers (port 53), otherwise via public resolvers (DoH over fixed IP addresses at several operators, plus port 53). One path is enough. If a DNS filter (DNS64 blocklist, Pi-hole, firewall) blocks some resolvers, the check uses the others.

dnscheck.ok_direct: The nameservers are reachable directly – DNS-01 works from here.
dnscheck.ok_public: The nameservers are not reachable directly (port 53 blocked or redirected), but public resolvers are – DNS-01 works from here.
dnscheck.none: No path reachable: neither the nameservers directly nor a public resolver. Enter a reachable resolver below or allow one of the resolvers in your DNS filter/firewall.
dnscheck.own_label: Additional resolvers for the check (one per line)
dnscheck.own_hint: IP address (port 53), IP:port or https://…, tls://…, quic://… (at most 10). They are added to the built-in resolvers and asked first. Empty = built-in only.

ports.docker_host: With --network host (network_mode: host) the ports apply directly on the host, without forwarding; then no other program on the host may use the same port. Recommended for PROXY64 streams, DNS64 and Honeypot64.

ports.pub_no_hint: Docker bridge network: PROXY64 listens inside the container, but the port is not published on the Docker host.

Publish the ports when starting the container, then recreate it:

Then you share the IPv4 address with other customers and cannot be reached through it from outside, even if DynDNS sets it correctly. This cannot be detected with certainty from inside, but is very likely here.

forwards.title: Forwarding
forwards.domain_hint: Applies to all names below, e.g. company.local, corp.example.com or a network like 192.168.0.0/16 (becomes the reverse zone).
forwards.servers_hint: One per line: IP (port 53), IP:port, tls://…, https://…/dns-query or quic://…; in order, the next one on failure.
forwards.test: Test (query the SOA of the domain)
forwards.builtin: Local names (.lan, .local, .fritz.box …) and private reverse lookups
forwards.order: Order: custom records, rewrites, forwarding, router, internet. Blocklists and group rules also apply to forwarded domains, except for local names and private reverse lookups. If none of the servers answers, the result is SERVFAIL – the name never goes to the internet.
forwards.rw_hint: DNS64 resolves the target itself and answers under the queried name (without CNAME). *.example.com applies to all names below.

dns64.title: DNS64
dns64.not_running: The DNS service is not running.

lists.title: Blocklists
lists.hint: Tick and apply; the DNS service then reloads the lists. “Domains” only counts entries not already in a list above.
lists.add_hint: Formats: hosts file, one domain per line or Adblock syntax (||domain^, exceptions @@||domain^).
lists.hint_categories: Lists marked “Child safety” and “Bypass” apply to all devices in the network; “Bypass” blocks foreign DoH servers, VPNs and proxies that devices could use to get around DNS64. The stronger levels (Pro++, Ultimate) block more, now and then also something wanted: then release the domain.

allow.title: Allowed domains
allow.not_running: The allowlist can be edited once the DNS service is running.
allow.import_hint: One domain per line, e.g. from the allowlist.txt of the old DNS64 container or a Pi-hole whitelist. Comments (#) and timestamps are ignored, existing entries stay.

up.title: Upstream servers
up.hint: Queries to the internet go encrypted to the configured servers: DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH), DNS-over-TLS (DoT) or DNS-over-QUIC (DoQ). “Fastest in” shows how often a server answered first.

cache.title: DNS cache
cache.hint: Popular domains are renewed shortly before they expire. Expired entries are served instantly for up to 1 hour and refreshed in the background.

settings.firefox_canary: Firefox uses DNS64 (switch off Firefox’s own DoH)
settings.firefox_canary_hint: DNS64 does not resolve use-application-dns.net; Firefox then switches off its built-in DoH and asks DNS64 – otherwise Firefox bypasses blocklists and groups. On by default, like Pi-hole.
settings.title: Settings
settings.port_hint: UDP and TCP. Devices on your network use this host's IP as DNS server, which only works with port 53. Other ports are for testing or when 53 is taken.
settings.router_none: No router found at the moment, local names are not resolved.
settings.router_hint: Names like fritz.box, .lan or single host names only go to this DNS server, never to the internet. IPv4 or IPv6 (link-local with interface too, e.g. fe80::1%eth0), with a port as IP:port or [IPv6]:port. Automatic: the IPv4 gateway, otherwise the IPv6 gateway.
settings.anonymize_hint: Shortened or not stored applies to new entries; device names and top clients are then limited or unavailable.
settings.allow_nets_hint: Private networks, Tailscale (100.64.0.0/10) and directly attached private networks and IPv6 /64s are always allowed. Add e.g. another IPv6 prefix or VPN networks here, one per line; 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 are not possible.
settings.allow_nets_public: Public networks entered ({nets}): DNS64 answers every device in them, strangers too. Only enter what really belongs to you, and never forward port 53/853 on your router.
settings.refused: {n} queries from foreign addresses refused since start, last {ip} ({time}).
settings.up_hint: Queries to the internet go encrypted to the ticked servers: DoH (HTTPS, port 443), DoT (TLS, port 853) or DoQ (QUIC, port 853). Each server's certificate is verified.
settings.up_mode_hint: Fastest: measures the ticked servers continuously and asks only the fastest (1–6) at once; the others are re-measured briefly every 30 s and step in when one hangs or fails. Parallel: every query to all (fast, but a lot of traffic). In order: always the first, the next only on error.
settings.up_add_hint: Plain DNS server: just the IP address, e.g. 8.8.8.8 (port 53) or 192.168.1.1:5353 – unencrypted. Encrypted: https://…/dns-query for DoH, tls://name[:853] for DoT, quic://name[:853] for DoQ. DNS64 needs the bootstrap IPs to reach an encrypted server without DNS (required when the address contains a name); the certificate is checked against the name.
settings.notify_upstream: Upstream server failing for more than 3 minutes and back again
settings.notify_lists: Blocklist failed to load three times in a row
settings.notify_hint: Sent to the default channels (not during quiet hours), set up under

records.local_only: This node only (not synced in the cluster)
records.comment_ph: optional, e.g. NAS in the basement
records.no_ptr: No reverse lookup (PTR) from this record
records.import_hint: Hosts file (IP and names per line), CSV (name,type,value,ttl,comment) or JSON. Existing records stay, localhost and 0.0.0.0 lines are skipped.

groups.schedules_hint: Uses the node’s time zone; end before start = across midnight (e.g. 21:00–07:00), equal = whole day. “Internet off”: only local names, custom records and the group’s releases work; pages show a notice from the node (for https:// only a certificate error). “Block” acts like “Internet off” at once, “Free” suspends schedules and categories for a while, blocklists keep applying.
groups.safesearch_hint: Searches only with SafeSearch, YouTube in restricted mode; cannot be switched off on the device. YouTube “off” = YouTube without restriction (block it with the streaming category).
groups.bypass_hint: Blocks foreign DoH servers, VPNs and proxies (HaGeZi list), switches off iCloud Private Relay and Firefox’s own DoH on these devices. Mobile data or a fixed foreign DNS still get around it.
groups.hint_rules: Each group has its own rules (expand “Rules”): blocklists like for all devices or an own selection, blocked categories, own releases and blocks. Devices without a group use the settings under “Blocklists”.
groups.cats_hint: Social networks, games and streaming are small lists maintained by Node64 (TikTok, Instagram, Roblox, Fortnite, YouTube, Netflix and more); gambling and adult content switch on the HaGeZi lists for the group. A release of the group always wins.
groups.domains_hint: Applies with subdomains. A release beats blocks, categories and blocklists, e.g. the school platform.
groups.title: Groups
groups.hint: Groups bundle devices, e.g. “Kids” or “Guests”. A device belongs to at most one group; if it matches several (e.g. by MAC and by network), the upper one wins.
groups.hint_mac: Devices are recognised by their MAC address first (the host’s neighbour table, IPv4 and IPv6), so they stay in their group even with a new IPv6 or IPv4 address. DNS64 only sees the MAC in the same network and with host networking; otherwise enter the IP address or a whole network (e.g. its own VLAN).
groups.label: Label
groups.devices_none: No queries in the last 24 hours.
groups.no_mac: MAC unknown (other network, bridge networking or device inactive for a while): assigned by IP
groups.anon_hint: The query log stores addresses shortened or not at all (Settings → Privacy). Devices cannot be picked here then; entries by MAC, IP or network in the group above still work.

enc.title: Encrypted on the home network
enc.hint: Devices ask DNS64 encrypted instead of port 53: DNS-over-HTTPS (browsers, Windows, iOS/macOS), DNS-over-TLS (iOS/macOS, Android) and DNS-over-QUIC. The same blocklists, allowlist and allowed networks apply.
enc.ports_hint: DoH uses HTTPS (TCP), DoT TCP and DoQ UDP; defaults are 443 and 853. The DoH port must not be the web interface port.
enc.names_hint: Names devices use to reach DNS64 (e.g. dns.home.lan, as a custom record pointing to the node's IP), one per line. The node's IPs are added to the certificate automatically.
enc.cert_hint: With the own CA, devices install the CA certificate once; it may only vouch for private addresses. Publicly valid without installing anything: Let's Encrypt (card on the right) or an own certificate via NODE64_TLS_CERT/NODE64_TLS_KEY.
enc.howto_apple: iPhone, iPad, Mac: download the profile, install it under Settings → General → VPN & Device Management and, with the own CA, trust it under About → Certificate Trust Settings.
enc.howto_windows: Windows 11: import the CA certificate into “Trusted Root Certification Authorities”, then set DNS manually to the node's IP with DNS-over-HTTPS and the DoH address above.
enc.howto_browser: Firefox/Chrome: secure DNS with the DoH address above; Firefox has its own certificate store (import the CA there).
enc.howto_android: Android “Private DNS” (DoT) only accepts publicly valid certificates, no own CA: set up Let's Encrypt above and enter the name as private DNS provider.
enc.cert_central_hint: Certificates (Let's Encrypt, own CA) are managed in the certificate management; it renews them and DNS64 picks them up without a restart.
enc.central_have: Certificate from the certificate management: {name} ({issuer}), valid until {date}.

acme.mig_failed: The move to the certificate management is still pending ({err}); until then DNS64 keeps serving the previous certificate but does not renew it. Next attempt at the next start.

settings.title: Settings
settings.profile_hint: A profile leaves out ports another part of Node64 already has open (e.g. PROXY64 on 80/443, DNS64 on 53/853, the web interface). With a custom selection a port in use is an error.
settings.services_hint: Only for “Custom selection”: one service and port per line, for http/https optionally a decoy ({pages}). Services: ssh, telnet, http, https, tcp.
settings.scan_hint: Detects sources that touch many trap ports within a short time.
settings.limits_hint: Concurrent connections; empty = default (8 per IP, 512 in total). Protects the node from overload.
settings.storage_hint: Older events and everything above the limit are deleted hourly (oldest first).
settings.notify_hint: At most one bundled message per hour with the count and the first IPs, via the default channels, set up under
settings.about_text: The trap services accept logins and always reject them. Nothing is executed, nothing is downloaded and no outgoing connection is made. Every touch is suspicious because no real service runs on these ports.
settings.report_hint: Every 10 minutes, source IPs, kinds, ports, credentials from the honeypot (user name and password), paths, user agents and the start of payloads are sent to ipv64 – never your own IP and no sources from private or reserved networks. From real logs (log sensor, syslog) only IP, kind, service, port, count and rule are sent. The data feeds into the v64 blocklist.
settings.local_block: Block detected attackers in PROXY64 (local block list)
settings.local_block_hint: IPs the honeypot detects as attackers (login attempts, exploits, port scans, scanners) are blocked by PROXY64 right away for all hosts and streams – even without reporting to ipv64. Never private addresses or exceptions. Duration and list:
settings.local_block_noproxy: PROXY64 is not running – nothing is blocked until PROXY64 is switched on.
settings.report_nokey: This needs the node's central ipv64 API key.
settings.hostname_hint: Shown in the Telnet prompt, the TLS certificate, page titles (Proxmox VE, NAS) and by Elasticsearch. Empty = generated from the sensor ID, different on every node and stable across restarts (here: {name}).

watch.title: Early warning
watch.intro: Add your own networks: if an IP from them shows up as an attacker at ipv64 (usually a hijacked device), the node tells you. The networks are stored at ipv64 and checked there after every scoring run; your DynDNS IPs are included automatically.
watch.nokey: The early warning needs the central ipv64 API key.
watch.auth_error: ipv64 rejected the API key. Check the key in the settings.
watch.load_error: The list could not be loaded from ipv64:
watch.limits: {used} of {max} networks · IPv4 from /{v4} · IPv6 from /{v6}
watch.label: Label
watch.verified_hint: ipv64 links this network to your account: every sighting is reported.
watch.unverified_hint: Without verification ipv64 only reports IPs that are on the v64 blocklist.
watch.full: All {max} networks of your account class are in use. Remove one to add another.
watch.add_hint: Single IP or network, e.g. 203.0.113.0/24 or 2001:db8:1::/48. Public addresses only.
watch.dyndns_hint: ipv64 watches the current IPs of your DynDNS domains automatically. They count as verified: every sighting is reported.
watch.no_dyndns: No DynDNS IPs in the account.

watch.auth_backoff: The API key was rejected. With the same key the node only asks every 6 hours; a new key or “Fetch now” tries right away.
watch.about_unverified: Networks without verification only report IPs that are on the v64 blocklist (which is public anyway). That way nobody can add other people's networks to spy on them.
watch.about_dyndns: Your DynDNS IPs and verified networks report every sighting by a sensor, even below the blocklist threshold.
watch.about_notify: The node fetches hits every 30 minutes and sends one bundled notification per fetch through your channels. You don't need a sensor of your own for this.
watch.hits_hint: The node keeps the last {count} hits.

logs.title: Log sensor and syslog
logs.intro: Reads logs of real services (SSH, web servers, mail, Proxmox, Nextcloud, Vaultwarden …) and accepts syslog from routers and firewalls. Bundled rules only report attacks above a threshold (e.g. 5 failed logins in 10 minutes); successful logins reset the counter.
logs.privacy: From real logs only IP, kind, service, port, count and rule are stored and reported – no user names, passwords, paths, user agents or other content.
logs.files_hint: Absolute paths or patterns (e.g. /host/log/nginx/*access.log) below {roots}; the bin button removes a file or pattern and saves. Mount the host logs with -v /var/log:/host/log:ro, for auth.log also --group-add 4. journald only via rsyslog or syslog forwarding.
logs.syslog_hint: UDP and TCP on the same port, empty = off (usually 514). Senders as IP or network (CIDR), one per line; empty = private networks and localhost only. UDP senders can be spoofed – do not expose the port to the internet.
logs.status: State of log sensor and syslog
logs.hint_perm: No read permission – the container needs --group-add 4 (group adm).

cat.title: Trap services
cat.intro: Switch on what should be online. Port and bait can be changed; the state shows whether the port is free, open or used by another part of Node64.
cat.unsaved: Template applied – not saved yet. Check it and confirm with “Save”.
cat.low_hint: Node64 opens ports below 1024 without root through the cap_net_bind_service capability (included in the image). If the container drops it (--cap-drop), these ports stay closed with “permission denied”.
cat.extra: More entries (a service can run several times)
cat.extra_hint: For example ssh additionally on 2200 or http with its own bait on 8081. Empty rows are ignored; new empty rows appear after saving.
cat.profile_hint: If the selection matches a template exactly, it is saved as that profile: new services of future versions are then added automatically, and ports another part has open are just left out. Otherwise it counts as a custom selection, and a used port is an error.
cat.node_hint: On a node with other modules some ports are already taken – e.g. 80/443 by PROXY64, 53/853 by DNS64 and {ui} by the Node64 interface. For all ports use a dedicated honeypot node: Node64 with only Honeypot64 (move the interface to an unusual port, NODE64_HTTP_PORT, default 8080 – itself a popular trap port) or the headless mode (NODE64_MODE=honeypot, info page on 9064).
cat.advanced: Advanced: selection as a text list
cat.advanced_hint: One service and port per line, for http/https optionally a bait ({pages}). Services: {services}. The list shows the same selection as the table; “Save text list” saves the list instead of the table.

svc.http: Web bait, answer per path (WordPress, phpMyAdmin, admin …)
svc.https: Web bait with TLS, answer per path
svc.tcp: Any TCP port: connection and first bytes
svc.smtps: SMTP over TLS (SMTPS): logins recorded and rejected, no relay
svc.imaps: IMAP over TLS (IMAPS): logins recorded and rejected
svc.pop3s: POP3 over TLS (POP3S): logins recorded and rejected

cat.persona_hint: The profile decides what a trap pretends to be: banner, headers, responses and certificate (e.g. nginx, Proxmox VE, OpenSSH Ubuntu, Dropbear, MariaDB). The default for port and decoy is preselected; every profile captures the same data.
cat.proxy_hint: Only via PROXY64: the honeypot opens no ports of its own. It only gets what PROXY64 passes on – requests that match no host and those recognised as malicious (blocklists, reported attackers, exploit patterns, AI bots). Which kinds is set in PROXY64. Switching on services here turns it into a custom selection.

cert.title: Certificate for decoy names
cert.hint: HTTPS traps with a web server profile (nginx, Apache) and the mail traps with TLS (SMTPS, IMAPS, POP3S) present this certificate from the certificate manager. Profiles that are self-signed in real life (Proxmox, Webmin, NAS, UniFi, routers, Grafana, Home Assistant, Elasticsearch) stay self-signed. If the certificate is missing or not issued yet, everything stays self-signed.
cert.uses_none: No enabled trap presents the certificate (enable HTTPS with nginx/Apache, SMTPS, IMAPS or POP3S, or list ports below).
cert.ports_hint: Optional: ports that present the certificate despite a self-signed profile (e.g. 8006 for Proxmox with its own certificate). Comma-separated.
cert.ct_hint: The names of a certificate are public in the Certificate Transparency logs – scanners read them there. Use a separate domain or subdomain just for the decoys, never your main domain or names of real services.
cert.unavailable: Without the certificate manager (e.g. in headless mode) all traps stay self-signed.
cert.create_title: Create a certificate for decoy names
cert.create_intro: Creates a certificate in the certificate manager for individual, plausible names (no wildcard), e.g. mail., vpn., cloud., portal. below an ipv64 domain. It is issued via DNS-01 through ipv64; port 80 stays a trap. The new certificate is selected right away.
cert.nokey: Enter the ipv64 API key in the settings first.
cert.names_hint: Prefixes or full names, comma-separated, at most 20. No *, not the domain itself.
cert.dns_hint: Public IPv4 and/or IPv6 of the node (A/AAAA) or a name for a CNAME (e.g. the DynDNS domain). Existing records of the names stay untouched. Empty = create the records yourself.
cert.created: Certificate for {names} created and selected; it is being issued in the background (see Certificates).
cert.created_unselected: Certificate for {names} created but not selected (check the settings and choose the certificate above).
cert.err_domains: ipv64 domains could not be loaded: {error}
cert.err_tos: Accept the Let's Encrypt terms of service under Certificates first.

login.title: Watch the Node64 login
login.intro: Failed logins at the node's own login (password, TOTP, passkey, SSO, API and MCP keys) are counted per IP. At the threshold (default {threshold} in {window} minutes) an event of rule node64/login@1 is recorded – without usernames or passwords – with a notification, an instant block via PROXY64 (if enabled there) and reporting to ipv64 (if enabled). Private and local addresses are only counted, never reported.
login.notify_hint: Through the node's notifications, at most one message every 10 minutes (further ones are counted in).
login.public_hint: Never expose the Node64 interface to the internet (no port forwarding for the web port). From outside use a VPN or PROXY64 with login and access list.
login.counts: failed logins since start: {fails} counted, {local} local (not reported)

mode.title: View
mode.simple_hint: Pick a template, forward the ports in your router, done. All settings are in expert mode.
mode.expert_hint: All settings: single services and ports, profiles, certificate, limits, log sensor and syslog.

simple.custom_hint: Put together in expert mode. Choosing a template here replaces this selection.

desc.proxy: The honeypot opens no ports of its own. PROXY64 hands it requests that match no host and requests recognised as malicious – and it reports the attackers.
desc.minimal: SSH and web – the two most attacked services.
desc.standard: The usual bot targets: SSH, Telnet, web, FTP, mail, databases, RDP, VNC, MikroTik, Proxmox VE, MQTT.
desc.full: All traps, including rare services and web interfaces – best on a dedicated honeypot node.

simple.open_ports: Forward these to this node in your router:
simple.no_ports: No ports needed – PROXY64 has to be running.
simple.ports_hint: Ports already used on this node (e.g. 80/443 by PROXY64, 53 by DNS64, {ui} by the web interface) are left out. The overview shows which traps are really open.

start.title: Start page of the web trap
start.hint: What bots see on “/” – including those PROXY64 hands to the honeypot. Both forms record the credentials entered.

live.title: Live
live.hint: Live: arcs show attacks of the last hour from the source to your sensor; when nothing new comes in, older ones are replayed (fainter).
live.empty: No attacks with a known country in the last hour.

country.title: Location of the sensor
country.hint: Target of the arcs on the live map, here and on ipv64.net. Only needed if the detected country is wrong (e.g. a hosting provider's server abroad). Affects only the display, not the rating of attackers.

check.remove_confirm: Delete the Healthchecks check of this guest?

mcp.title: AI interface (MCP)
mcp.intro: With the Model Context Protocol (MCP), AI applications such as Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code or Claude Desktop can query the state of this node: checks, Proxmox, DNS64, PROXY64, Honeypot64, DynDNS, certificates, notifications and logs. Read-only – the AI cannot change anything.
mcp.lan_only: Home network only: requests from public addresses (also via PROXY64 or a reverse proxy) are rejected with 403. Private networks, VPN (e.g. 100.64.0.0/10) and localhost are allowed.
mcp.lan_only_this: This browser connects from {ip} – not a private address. An AI application at this location would be rejected.
mcp.switch_hint: When switched off, /mcp answers 404. Keys are kept.
mcp.url_hint: Transport "Streamable HTTP" on the port of the web interface, same certificate. Send the key in the header "Authorization: Bearer …".
mcp.keys_hint: Separate keys only for /mcp, independent of the API keys. For each key you choose which areas the AI may read. At most 60 requests per minute per key.
mcp.key_show_once: The key is shown only now – copy it into the setup of your AI application.
mcp.key_invalid: Please enter a name (at most 100 characters) and select at least one area.
mcp.revoke_confirm: Revoke this key? Applications using it lose access immediately.
mcp.setup_placeholder: Replace <MCP-KEY> with your key. Right after creating a key it is already filled in here.
mcp.setup_with_key: With your new key – just copy.
mcp.setup_claude_code: Run in a terminal (add --scope user for all projects):
mcp.setup_cursor: In ~/.cursor/mcp.json (all projects) or .cursor/mcp.json in the project:
mcp.setup_vscode: In .vscode/mcp.json in the project (or "MCP: Open User Configuration"):
mcp.setup_claude_desktop: In claude_desktop_config.json (Settings › Developer › Edit config). Claude Desktop connects remote servers as "Connectors" from the cloud – they cannot reach your home network. Hence the local bridge mcp-remote (requires Node.js).
mcp.setup_tls: With the node's self-signed certificate, Node.js applications (Claude Code, mcp-remote) reject the connection: download the node certificate and set NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/node64.pem, or select a certificate from the certificate management for the web interface.
mcp.sec_read_only: Read-only tools; nothing can be changed via MCP.
mcp.sec_no_secrets: No secrets: no keys, tokens, passwords, private keys or channel credentials in the responses.
mcp.sec_untrusted: Third-party data (honeypot, DNS queries, paths, user agents, VM names, response texts) is marked under "untrusted"; the AI is told never to treat it as instructions.
mcp.sec_limits: Private networks only, 60 requests per minute per key, limited results.
mcp.sec_audit: Every tool call is recorded in the audit log with key and parameters.
mcp.settings_hint: AI applications (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code …) read the state of the node via MCP – home network only, read-only.

healthchecks.desc: Monitors websites, servers and services locally in your home network and optionally online from ipv64 – with notifications on outages and recovery.

healthchecks.h2: Status pages, maintenance windows and many notification channels

dyndns.h1: IPv4 and IPv6, including prefixes for devices in your network
dyndns.h2: Reports failed updates and IP changes

cdn64.desc: Reverse proxy for the services in your home network: names with HTTPS certificates, access protection and forwarding – locally or via the ipv64 CDN64 servers.

cdn64.h2: Reachable even without open ports via the CDN64 servers

sonar64.title: Sonar64
sonar64.intro: Community measurement network: nodes at participants' homes measure each other and the ipv64 anchors – sparingly, following a signed plan from ipv64.net and within fixed limits. The results appear on the public map at ipv64.net/sonar.

participate.title: Participation
participate.text: By participating, this node becomes a Sonar64 node. It measures response times to other nodes and to the anchors and reports them, signed, to ipv64 every 5 minutes.
participate.p1: Targets only come from the signed plan from ipv64, never private networks; a few packets per second, fixed daily limit.
participate.p2: Public are display name, provider, access type, trust level and the location blurred to about 1 km – never your IP address.
participate.p3: The default is "outbound only": others only measure you once you choose "also measured".
participate.nokey: To participate, Node64 needs the central ipv64 API key (a dedicated Sonar token is created from it).
participate.off_confirm: Stop participating in Sonar64? The node will no longer measure or answer on UDP 6464.

status.port_busy: UDP {port} is in use – the node only measures outbound.

trust.title: Trust level
trust.quarantine_text: Your measurements currently do not count (too many implausible values). The node keeps measuring; ipv64 re-checks daily.

trust_hint.new: Less than 7 days in – your values count little so far.
trust_hint.trusted: Counts double and is a reference for neighbours.
trust_hint.pillar: Reference target for new nodes, high weight for outages.
trust_hint.anchor: Fixed measurement point run by ipv64.
trust_hint.quarantine: Keeps measuring but does not count.

settings.title: Measurement
settings.outbound_hint: The node measures others and the anchors but is never planned as a target itself.
settings.measured_hint: The node answers on UDP {port} (forward the port in your router) or the router answers pings. That way your line is measured as well.
settings.measured_ip: Then some other participants see your public IP address (only the nodes that measure you according to the plan; never public).
settings.budget_hint: Upper limit per round (every 5 minutes) and day; ipv64 plans below it.
settings.quiet_hint: Hours without measuring in local time, e.g. 23-6; empty = none.
